summary: Describes paging, in which an idle mobile host is alerted when traffic arrives. It assesses the need for IP paging and gives recommendations for the Seamoby working group's charter.

plainLanguage.summary: A sleeping phone needs a tap on the shoulder when someone is calling. This asks how the network should tap it.

questions: why is paging needed for mobile ip
subtitle: Alerting sleeping mobile devices when data arrives over IP.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices in power-saving mode cannot listen for incoming traffic all the time, but existing IP mobility protocols could not efficiently locate and alert them.
tldr.mechanism: IP paging uses a signaling protocol to alert dormant mobile devices that traffic has arrived, triggering them to wake up and establish a connection to receive that traffic.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends that the Seamoby working group develop an IP paging protocol, particularly for scenarios where subnets do not map cleanly to radio paging areas.

facts.value: Problem statement for Seamoby working group

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: Mobile IPv4, Mobile IPv6, and radio link support

today: IP paging was standardized in RFC 5191 (Mobile IP Paging Support), which provides mechanisms for locating and alerting dormant mobile devices. The document remains informational and represents a snapshot of wireless technology concerns from 2001.

sections.title: Dormant Mode and Power Saving
sections.content:
Mobile devices can save power by entering dormant mode, where they reduce monitoring of radio channels rather than listening constantly. This reduces both battery drain and signaling load on the network. In existing radio protocols, there are two approaches. Some protocols support dormant mode only, where a dormant device periodically wakes up on a schedule and its associated radio access point delivers any buffered traffic. Others support paging, where the radio access points are grouped into paging areas, and when a packet arrives for a dormant device, the network sends a signal on a dedicated paging channel to wake it up, rather than having it wake on a fixed schedule.

The question this document addresses is whether IP-layer protocols (Mobile IPv4 and Mobile IPv6) need to support paging themselves, or whether existing mechanisms suffice.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones in dormant mode take naps to save battery. The network can either let them wake up on a timer, or tap them on the shoulder when something arrives. The question is: does the network need a special knock on the shoulder at the IP level, or do existing methods work?

sections.title: Paging Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
Understanding paging requires several key concepts. Dormant mode is a state where the mobile restricts monitoring of radio channels. Time-slotted dormant mode is when the mobile alternates between sleeping and waking periods, synchronized with the network so it listens when traffic arrives. A paging area is a collection of radio access points signaled together to locate a dormant device. Paging area registrations are signals a dormant device sends when crossing a paging area boundary to tell the network where it is. A paging channel is a radio channel dedicated to alerting dormant devices, separate from the traffic channel. The traffic channel carries normal IP data for active devices.

In radio protocols without paging support, the network always knows exactly where a device is (at which access point it last registered). Packets are buffered at that access point and delivered when the device wakes. In radio protocols with paging support, the network only knows which paging area a device is in, so it must page the entire area when a packet arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: Paging areas are neighborhoods. When your phone is asleep in a neighborhood, the network doesn't know which house you're in, so it sends a signal to the whole neighborhood: "Wake up if you're there." If the network always knew your exact house, it would just tap that house.

sections.title: When IP Paging Is Necessary
sections.content: The document analyzes whether Mobile IP needs IP paging. For radio protocols without paging, Mobile IP does not need paging because the network knows the mobile's exact location at all times. For homogeneous networks (all one radio technology) with paging support, the analysis depends on how paging areas map to IP subnets. When paging area boundaries match subnet boundaries, or when multiple paging areas are in one subnet, Mobile IP registration on paging area updates can work without a separate IP paging protocol. However, when multiple subnets map to a single paging area, a mobile can move between subnets while dormant, making it invisible to IP routing. In this case, a packet sent to the mobile's last known subnet may arrive at the wrong access point, while the mobile has moved to a different subnet but cannot signal it. This creates unnecessary latency before the mobile can be reached. IP paging would solve this by having a paging agent in the paging area handle the alert, reducing initial connection latency. For heterogeneous networks (multiple radio technologies), the complexity multiplies, and IP paging becomes more attractive as a way to abstract away technology-specific details.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone always tells the network exactly which room it's in, no special wake-up protocol is needed. But if it only knows what building it's in, and wanders between offices in that building while asleep, the network might send data to the wrong office. A special knock on the door for that building helps.

sections.title: The Practical Case
sections.content: While theoretical analysis shows Mobile IP could handle most scenarios with enhancements, practical reality is messier. Network operators often do not enable paging area registrations; instead they use heuristics (educated guesses) about where to page for a mobile. When registrations are not enabled, Mobile IP registrations cannot use them as a transport, leaving no IP-level signaling for paging. Additionally, mapping of paging areas to subnets is often arbitrary, with overlaps and no clear subset relationships. Requiring operators to redesign their networks to create clean mappings is unrealistic. Finally, different mobile terminals in the same area might be assigned different paging area identifiers by the radio protocol. Working through all these practical cases would produce a more complex result than simply defining an IP paging protocol that allows a home agent or hierarchical agent to signal a paging agent in the paging area when a packet arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: In theory, the existing system could handle it with more tricks. But in practice, network operators run things differently and messier. A simple IP-level knock is cleaner than trying to handle all the special cases.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content: The document recommends that the Seamoby working group undertake work on IP paging in four areas. First, protocol work is necessary to define a way for the network to find a mobile in dormant mode in the identified deployment scenarios. Second, this work should be pursued in a way consistent with Mobile IP and other IETF protocols, with recommendations for how to achieve the best match between radio paging protocols and IP. Third, if Seamoby decides to pursue a micromobility protocol that requires paging, paging protocol design should be undertaken within that context. Fourth, the working group should write a Best Current Practice document explaining how to map IP subnets to paging areas and which techniques to use when, to guide network designers in wireless networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The document suggests the networking group should: build an IP wake-up protocol that works with Mobile IP, write instructions on how to map networks properly for paging, and prepare for future protocols that might need paging too.
